---
title: "Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel Test in SAS"
---

# Introduction

The Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) procedure tests for conditional independence in partial contingency tables for a 2 x 2 x K design. However, it can be generalized to tables of X x Y x K dimensions. This page also briefly discusses derivation of risk differences and their confidence intervals which often accompany a CMH test.

The CMH test is calculated in SAS using the `PROC FREQ` procedure. By default, it outputs the chi square statistic, degrees of freedom and p-value for each of the three alternative hypotheses: `general association`, `row means differ`, and `nonzero correlation`. It is up to the statistical analyst or statistician to know which result is appropriate for their analysis.

When the design of the contingency table is 2 x 2 x K (i.e, X == 2 levels, Y == 2 levels, K \>= 2 levels), the three test statistics listed above are identical, and in this special case the SAS output also includes the Mantel-Haenszel Common Odds Ratio (odds ratio estimate, 95% CI, P-value) and the Breslow-Day Test for Homogeneity of the Odds Ratios (chi-square statistic, degrees of freedom, P-value).

Below is the syntax to conduct a CMH analysis in SAS:

``` sas
proc freq data = filtered_data; 
    tables K * X * Y / cmh; 
    * the order of K, X, and Y appearing on the line is important!;
    * K = stratum, X = row, Y = column;
run; 
```

# Data used

The adcibc data described [here](https://psiaims.github.io/CAMIS/R/cmh.html) is used for this example.

``` sas
proc import datafile = 'data/adcibc.csv'
    out = adcibc
    dbms = csv
    replace;
    getnames = yes;
    guessingrows = max;
run;
```

# Code used

The basic code used is shown below.

``` sas
proc freq data = adcibc; 
    tables agegr1 * trtp *  sex / cmh;  
run;
```

## Example 1: 2 x 2 x 2 (i.e, X = 2 TRT levels, Y = 2 SEX levels, K = 2 AGE levels)

Let's test if there is a difference between 2 of the treatments (Placebo, and high dose), in the proportion of females, whilst adjusting for 2 levels of Age group (\<65 and 65-\<80). NOTE: using a `where` statement, we have removed data in the low dose and \>80 categories.

``` sas
proc freq data = adcibc(where = (trtpn ne 54 and agegr1 ne ">80")); 
    tables agegr1 * trtp *  sex / cmh;  
run;
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: 50%
knitr::include_graphics("../images/cmh/saspage_output1.png")
```

## Example 2: 3 x 2 x K (i.e, X = 3 levels, Y = 2 levels, K \>= 2 levels)

Let's test if there is a difference across all 3 treatments (Placebo, Xanomeline low dose and high dose), in the proportion of females, whilst adjusting for all 3 levels of Age group (\<65, 65-\<80 and \>=80). Here K=Agegrp1 the stratification variable we are controlling for, X=Treatment -what we want to compare, and Y=Sex the binary outcome variable we want to see if it's different between treatments (often this would be response/ non-response!).

``` sas
proc freq data = adcibc; 
    tables agegr1 * trtp *  sex / cmh;  
run;
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: 50%
knitr::include_graphics("../images/cmh/saspage_output2.png")
```

# Estimating treatment effects within strata and combined across strata

The CMH tests identify whether there are differences in the column variable response between rows while controlling for the stratification factor. However we may want to get an estimate of the direction and size of treatment effect (with CI), either within each stratum or combined across strata.

## Risk Differences and other contrasts for each stratum

For more details on this topic, see the section on analysis of [CIs for independent proportions](https://psiaims.github.io/CAMIS/SAS/ci_for_2indep_prop.html)

Risk differences within each stratum (for 2 x 2 x K tables) can be obtained by adding the `riskdiff` option in SAS. The exact same output is obtained as per example 1 above, with the addition of 2 tables (1 for each age stratum), showing the proportion of Female patients within each treatment (with 95% CIs), and the difference in proportions between the treatments (with 95% CI). By default, the CIs are calculated using Wald asymptotic confidence limits and in addition, the 'exact' Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals for the risks. See the SAS User Guide [here](https://support.sas.com/documentation/cdl/en/procstat/67528/HTML/default/viewer.htm#procstat_freq_details53.htm) and [here](https://support.sas.com/documentation/cdl/en/procstat/67528/HTML/default/viewer.htm#procstat_freq_details53.htm) for more detail on the range of CIs SAS can calculate for the risk differences.

Similarly, estimates of per-stratum Relative Risk and Odds Ratio may be obtained using the `relrisk` and `oddsratio` options.

The individual treatment comparisons within strata can be useful to explore if the treatment effect is in the same direction and size for each stratum, such as to determine if pooling them is in fact sensible.

``` sas
# Default method is: Wald asymptotic confidence limits 
proc freq data = adcibc (where=(trtpn ne 54 and agegr1 ne ">80")); 
    tables  agegr1 * trtp *  sex / cmh riskdiff; 
run; 
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: 50%
knitr::include_graphics("../images/cmh/saspage_output3.png")
```

Note above that exact CIs are not output for the difference between the treatments. You can request SAS output other CI methods as shown below. This example outputs the risk difference between the treatments and 95% CI, calculated for each age group stratum separately using the Miettinen-Nurminen (score) (MN) method.

``` sas
# You can change the confidence limits derivation using (CL=xxx) option
proc freq data = adcibc (where=(trtpn ne 54 and agegr1 ne "\>80")); 
    tables agegr1 * trtp * sex / cmh riskdiff(CL=MN);
run;
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: 50%
knitr::include_graphics("../images/cmh/saspage_output3b.png")
```

The per-stratum estimates & CIs can also be visualised on a forest plot, using the `plots=riskdiffplot(CL=MN)` option (or `relriskplot`/`oddsratioplot` for RR and OR respectively).

### SAS Common error: Make sure you output the risk difference for the correct level!

Including either `column=1` or `column=2` tells SAS which is your outcome of interest (ie, often that you want to compare treatment responders and not treatment non-responders!) By default it takes the 1st column sorted alphabetically but you can change this as shown below.

Note that if the data are such that there are no responses in either treatment group, the cross-tabulation will only have 1 column, and SAS PROC FREQ will fail to produce a confidence interval. In this unusual situation however, a valid confidence interval can (and should) still be produced for Risk Difference, which may be obtained using the %SCORECI macro available at [https://github.com/petelaud/ratesci-sas/tree/main](#0).

``` sas
proc freq data = adcibc (where=(trtpn ne 54 and agegr1 ne "\>80")); 
    tables agegr1 * trtp * sex / cmh riskdiff(common column=2);
run;
```

## Common Risk Differences across strata

For more details on this topic, see the section on analysis of [stratified proportions](https://psiaims.github.io/CAMIS/SAS/ci_for_prop_stratified.html).

### SAS Common error: SAS v9.4 cannot do a stratified Miettinen-Nurminen (score) confidence interval (but SAS Viya can)!

You may think by running the following code, that you would be creating a common risk difference using the stratified Miettinen-Nurminen (MN) method. However, the `CL=MN` option only implements the MN method for the per-stratum estimates, **not** the common RD estimate.

``` sas
# Specifying the Miettinen-Nurminen (score) method for per-stratum estimates; 
proc freq data = adcibc (where=(trtpn ne 54 and agegr1 ne ">80")); 
    tables  agegr1 * trtp *  sex / cmh riskdiff(common CL=MN); 
run; 
```

The output contains the risk difference CIs calculated for each stratum separately, and then a common risk difference using the 'summary score estimate' which combines the per-stratum CIs, and another CI using the Mantel-Haenszel method with a Sato variance estimate as shown below. Neither of these are stratified intervals, and they both have the potential to contradict the result of the CMH test. See the [SAS Procedures Guide](https://support.sas.com/documentation/cdl/en/procstat/67528/HTML/default/viewer.htm#procstat_freq_details63.htm) for more detail.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| out-width: 50%
knitr::include_graphics("../images/cmh/saspage_output3c.png")
```

`PROC FREQ` in the SAS Viya platform has introduced a new option `COMMONRISKDIFF(CL=MN)` that **does** use the stratified MN method (or `...(CL=MNMH)` with simpler MH weights). But there is no corresponding option for producing estimates of common RR or OR using the stratified MN method. The `COMMONRISKDIFF` option is also included in more recent implementations of SAS/STAT (14.3 onwards) on Base SAS 9.4, but without the `CL=MN` and `CL=MNMH` sub-options. The alternative `CL=MH` and `CL=SCORE` produce the same results as the `RISKDIFF(common)` option.

``` sas
# Specifying the stratified Miettinen-Nurminen (score) method in SAS Viya;
proc freq data = adcibc (where=(trtpn ne 54 and agegr1 ne ">80")); 
    tables  agegr1 * trtp *  sex / cmh commonriskdiff(CL=MN); 
run; 
```
